segments.speaker: A
segments.text: I'm Marcus, this is Iris. Last chapter was responsible engineering — the obligations a system owes the people it affects. Today we close the book: the conclusion, which makes the whole thesis quantitative. It opens with a failure story: an image classifier deployed across a fleet of mobile devices.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Three teams, and every one of them hit its metric. The architecture team chose depthwise separable convolutions. The compression team quantized to INT8 so everything fit in on-chip SRAM. The serving team held end-to-end p99 under fifty milliseconds. All green.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And then within weeks, accuracy fell four percentage points — on specific firmware and device cohorts only.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And nothing failed in isolation. INT8 quantization fixes its clipping ranges during calibration — it permanently encodes the distribution of the calibration images. A firmware-specific preprocessing routine interpolated images differently. On those cohorts the input distribution shifted, the calibrated ranges were wrong, and accuracy dropped.

visual.title: Local wins compose into a global loss
visual.alt: Three teams each hit their local metric — architecture (depthwise), compression (INT8 in SRAM), serving (p99 under 50 ms). A calibration choice then travels three stages downstream: INT8 clipping ranges meet a firmware-specific preprocessing path, the input distribution shifts on one cohort, and accuracy drops four points where nobody measured.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So no component broke, nothing crashed — and the monitoring never saw it because accuracy was only measured as an aggregate scalar over an offline eval set.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Exactly. The chapter's point: the failure lived at an interface no component test exercises. Per-cohort accuracy tracking from day one would have fired in week one. That's the opening argument for the thesis: the system is the model — the behavior a user receives comes from the pipeline, the weights, the execution stack, the serving path and the monitoring loop together. Never the weights alone.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The model as a file of floats is the wrong object to test, version and monitor.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Right. And the way the chapter makes that claim predictive is the five lighthouse models — each one a different limiting term.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Walk me through them.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: ResNet-50 is compute-bound — batching and reduced precision pay, extra bandwidth past the ridge is wasted. GPT-2 and Llama decode is bandwidth-bound — batching, fewer bytes per weight and KV-cache management pay; peak arithmetic at batch one is wasted. DLRM is capacity-bound — the embedding tables exceed one accelerator's memory, so sharding and caching pay and faster dense math is wasted. MobileNetV2 is compute-bound inside a phone power envelope — depthwise, then INT8. And keyword spotting is power-bound — a sub-megabyte INT8 model under a milliwatt beats streaming audio to the cloud, because the radio costs more energy than local inference.

visual.title: Five lighthouses, five limiting terms
visual.alt: Each lighthouse saturates one resource first. ResNet-50 compute, GPT-2/Llama decode bandwidth, DLRM memory capacity, MobileNetV2 compute inside a power envelope, keyword spotting energy. Each row names the lever that paid and the lever that was wasted.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And the regime isn't a property of the model name — it's the workload on a machine.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: That's the subtlety. GPT-2 training is compute-bound even though its decode is bandwidth-bound, because a training step reuses each weight across the batch. Precision moves it too: INT8 doubles the H100's peak rate without raising bandwidth, so the ridge point doubles — a layer whose activations still move at sixteen bits can fall below the new ridge and become bandwidth-bound.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: MobileNetV2 on an H100 instead of a phone NPU — same crossing.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Same crossing. Compute-bound on the NPU, memory-bound on the H100. And the chapter walks MobileNetV2 through nine phases of the book — the deployment tier sets the watt envelope, depthwise convolutions cut FLOPs eight-point-seven times on a representative layer and thirteen-point-seven times versus ResNet-50 overall, training at high throughput for a model that will serve single requests, capacity-matched augmentation, INT8 — where FP32 costs four times the bytes and FP16 two times — then mapping, benchmarking, serving, and monitoring. Every decision narrowed what the next phase could choose.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Then the chapter takes its thirteen quantitative principles and re-sorts them by the three questions the introduction asked.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: What shapes predictions — data-as-code and the bias feedback model. What limits execution — data gravity, the iron law, the silicon contract, the Pareto frontier, arithmetic intensity, energy movement, Amdahl. What evidence supports deployment — the verification gap, statistical drift, training-serving skew, and the latency budget.

visual.title: Thirteen principles, three questions
visual.alt: The thirteen quantitative principles sorted by the three questions of the introduction. What shapes predictions: data-as-code and bias feedback. What limits execution: data gravity, iron law, silicon contract, Pareto frontier, arithmetic intensity, energy movement, Amdahl. What evidence supports deployment: verification gap, statistical drift, training-serving skew, latency budget. Kinds marked: bound, decomposition, fitted model, policy, heuristic.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And they're not all the same kind of statement.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Right — three are hard bounds, two are decompositions, two fitted models, two policies, and four heuristics. The silicon contract is a heuristic: it predicts which resource saturates first, and the arithmetic intensity bound is what tests that prediction. Each principle only holds inside its stated assumptions.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: And the meta-principle above all of them is conservation of complexity — Tesler's law.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: A diagnostic, not a physical law: simplifying one part tends to move complexity somewhere else. Pruning spends capacity, quantization spends precision, distillation spends compute. After any local simplification, trace where the cost landed.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The energy-movement principle puts a number on the most basic asymmetry: one DRAM access costs about a hundred seventy-three to five hundred eighty-two times one arithmetic operation.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: FP32 sits at the low end of that range, FP16 sets the high end. Data movement dominates both the time ledger and the energy ledger — which is why it shows up everywhere.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Then the dual mandate gets measured on two lighthouses — trustworthy behavior on DLRM, physical deliverability on the GPT-2 family.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And the sharpest physics in the chapter: Llama 2 seventy-B at batch one. About forty-seven times GPT-2's parameters — a hundred forty gigabytes of FP16 weights, a hundred forty gigaflops per token. On two H100s — six point seven terabytes per second of aggregate bandwidth, nearly two thousand teraflops of FP16 peak — the memory floor is twenty-point-nine milliseconds and the compute floor is point-zero-seven. Two hundred ninety-five times apart.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: So a batch-one token is almost entirely a memory wait. The levers are batching, shrinking bytes per weight, or speculative decode — spending compute to get more tokens per weight read. Nothing else touches it.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And the serving side of the same lesson: an LLM chat endpoint with a fifty-millisecond mean time to first token — looks healthy — but a two-thousand-millisecond p99. A tail forty times the mean, against a two-hundred-millisecond SLO. Prompt processing and queueing behind long generations do that while the mean stays green.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Both halves of the mandate are budgets the system keeps meeting, not certificates earned at launch.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: Then future directions — the same principles stretched into new contexts. The edge under watt budgets, TinyML in kilobytes and milliwatts, and composed services where a request fans out through retrieval, a planner, tools, a generator and a verifier.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The latency of a composed request follows its critical path — parallel tool calls collapse to the slower one, not a sum.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And at fleet scale: a single GPU at about five point seven years mean time to failure. A thousand-twenty-four-accelerator pool — the cluster sees a failure about every forty-eight point eight hours. Roughly every two days.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: Fault tolerance stops being a property and becomes a requirement.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: The closing section puts the responsibility where the physics put it: robust systems assume confident-and-wrong is normal and build graceful degradation in — fallback paths, uncertainty thresholds, scoped rollback. And the fallacies all share one root: treating the system as decomposable into independent parts.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The Amdahl one is the arithmetic version: accelerate inference — ten percent of the request path — by ten times, and the system speeds up about ten percent.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: And the accuracy-version: a ninety-five percent model at five hundred milliseconds is infeasible under a hundred-millisecond SLO, while a ninety-three percent model at fifty ships. Feasibility first, then quality inside the feasible set.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: The book ends by tracing that voice-assistant request through every layer one last time.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: A keyword spotter — about two hundred thousand parameters, two hundred kilobytes of INT8 in one megabyte of flash, twenty megaflops, a milliwatt budget — listens for the wake word. Power-bound. A front end of MobileNetV2's size — six hundred megaflops on three and a half megabytes of INT8 inside five watts — transcribes on the NPU. DLRM ranks the retrieval against a hundred gigabytes of embeddings that exceed one H100's eighty — capacity before arithmetic. And GPT-2 writes the answer, reading three gigabytes of FP16 per token, a zero-point-nine millisecond memory floor. Power, compute, capacity, bandwidth — each stage bound by a different term of the same law.

visual.title: One request, four limiting terms
visual.alt: The voice-assistant request traced through the lighthouses. Wake word: KWS, 200 KB INT8 in 1 MB flash, 20 MFLOP under a milliwatt — power-bound. Speech front end on the phone NPU: 600 MFLOP on 3.5 MB INT8 inside 5 W — compute-in-envelope. Ranking: DLRM's 100 GB of embeddings exceed one H100's 80 GB — capacity-bound. Response: GPT-2 decode reads 3 GB of FP16 per token, a 0.9 ms memory floor — bandwidth-bound.

segments.speaker: A
segments.text: That's the book: the system is the model, the regime picks the lever, and the interfaces are where it breaks.

segments.speaker: B
segments.text: What endures is the method — start from empirical evidence and physical bounds, quantify the trade-offs, and treat system design as constrained optimization. The world is rushing to build AI systems; the task is to engineer them.
